lead: The embedded development life cycle (EDLC) is the ordered set of stages a firmware product passes through from the first customer need to the last field update: requirements, specification, architecture, implementation, integration and test, maintenance. It exists because embedded code is hard to change once it ships — a controller soldered into a washing machine or a braking ECU in a car cannot be patched like a phone app. Each stage hands over a written deliverable that gets reviewed, so mistakes are caught while they are still cheap. Every firmware project, from a UPI payment terminal to a smart meter, runs some version of it.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the coding stage, Chapter 6.3 for target testing, and Unit 1 for design metrics such as cost, power and time-to-market.

sections.h3: The stages and what each one delivers

blocks.text: Each EDLC stage takes the previous stage's output, adds detail, and produces a deliverable. A review checks that deliverable before the next stage starts. This is the cheap place to catch an error: a wrong requirement fixed during coding costs hours, and the same error found after a product recall costs crores.

items: Requirements: what the system must do, in the customer's words. Deliverable: a numbered requirement list with quantities (response within 10 ms, battery life 6 months).
Specification: the same needs written so they can be checked. Deliverable: a functional specification with inputs, outputs and limits.
Architecture: block diagram of hardware and software, processor choice, task split. Deliverable: an architecture document.
Implementation: writing and unit-testing the modules, as in Chapter 6.1.
Integration and test: joining modules on the real board and proving the system meets the specification.
Maintenance: fixing defects and adding features after release.

blocks.text: The planned schedule adds the stage durations. This gives the delivery date the customer sees.
T_total = T_req + T_spec + T_arch + T_impl + T_int + T_test
blocks.where: T_req, T_spec, T_arch, T_impl, T_int, T_test are the calendar weeks planned for each stage on the project Gantt chart; T_total is the time from project start to customer delivery, not the total person-effort. The sum holds only when the stages run one after another. When two adjacent stages overlap by n weeks, subtract n weeks once from the sum. Maintenance is left out because T_total is measured up to customer delivery.

sections.h3: Life cycle models and how they differ

blocks.text: Waterfall runs the six stages once, in sequence, with a review gate between each pair. It suits projects where the requirements are stable and the product is safety-critical, such as an infusion pump. Its weakness is that any late change forces the team back up the chain.

The V-model is waterfall bent into a V. The left leg decomposes the design: requirements, then specification, then architecture, then module design. The right leg integrates and tests upward. The rule that defines the V is that each test level is planned as soon as its matching design level is written: module design pairs with unit test, architecture with integration test, specification with system test, and requirements with acceptance test. Test planning therefore starts in week one, not after coding.

Spiral repeats the whole cycle in risk-driven loops. Each loop ends with a prototype and a risk review, so the riskiest part (often new hardware) is proved first. It fits products where both the chip and the software are new, a situation covered in Chapter 6.5.

Agile uses short iterations of one to four weeks, each ending in runnable code, and lets requirements change between iterations. It fits consumer IoT products. It is used less for certified safety software, where every change must be re-verified before release.

Verification asks whether the product is being built right: does each artifact match the specification it was derived from? For a test level in the V-model, that is the design level it is paired with. Reviews, inspections and unit tests are verification. Validation asks whether the right product is being built: does the finished system meet the customer's need? Acceptance tests and field trials are validation. A design can pass every verification step and still fail validation if the requirement itself was wrong.

Integration joins tested modules into the full system. Big-bang integration switches everything on at once and makes a fault hard to locate. Top-down integration starts at the main control flow and replaces missing lower modules with stubs, small dummy routines that accept the call and return a fixed value. Bottom-up integration starts at the leaf modules, the lowest-level drivers and hardware-access routines, and tests them with drivers, small test programs that call the module under test and supply its inputs. Sandwich integration does both ends and meets in the middle. Whichever is chosen, integration is a planned stage with its own schedule, not an afternoon at the end.

items: Configuration management keeps every file under version control and tags each release, so the exact binary shipped to a customer can be rebuilt later.
A traceability matrix maps each requirement to a design section, a code module and a test case; a blank cell is a defect in the process.
Documentation covers the requirement list, architecture, test plan, test results and release note.

Maintenance is corrective (fix defects), adaptive (new hardware or OS), perfective (new features) and preventive (clean-up). It usually costs more than the original development, and its change requests re-enter the life cycle at the requirements stage.

figure.caption: Each stage hands a reviewed deliverable to the next, and the planned weeks are those of the worked example. The dashed edge is the change path: a defect report or a new requirement sends the project back to requirements.

spec.title: EDLC stages
spec.aria: A development flow goes from requirements through specification, architecture, implementation, integration and test to maintenance, with a dashed change edge back to requirements.

examples.question: A team plans firmware for a smart water meter. Planned durations: requirements 2 weeks, specification and architecture together 3 weeks, coding 6 weeks, integration 3 weeks, system test 2 weeks. (a) Find the total schedule in a pure waterfall. (b) The team starts integration one week before coding ends, so coding and integration overlap by 1 week, with no change to the other stages. Find the new total and the percentage saving.
steps: List the stage durations in order: 2, 3, 6, 3, 2 weeks.
An overlap of 1 week means that week is counted once instead of twice, so subtract it once: 16 - 1 = 15 weeks.
examples.answer: Waterfall total is 16 weeks; with a 1-week overlap between coding and integration the total becomes 15 weeks, a saving of 6.25 percent.
examples.check:
req = 2
des = 3
code = 6
integ = 3
test = 2
total = req + des + code + integ + test
overlap = 1
overlapped = total - overlap
saving = overlap / total * 100
print(total)
print(overlapped)
print(saving)

traps: Treating testing as one final phase. Integration and system test are separate planned stages with their own weeks, and in the V-model their planning starts with the matching design stage.
Forgetting maintenance and documentation. The life cycle runs past the ship date, and maintenance change requests re-enter at requirements.

Confusing verification with validation. Verification compares an artifact with the specification it was derived from (in the V-model, the design level it is paired with); validation compares the product with the customer's need.
Overlapping schedules twice. An overlap of n weeks subtracts n weeks once from the sum, not once for each of the two stages.
Assuming a shorter total means a cheaper project. Overlap adds coordination effort even when calendar weeks fall.

quiz.q: List the six EDLC stages in order.
quiz.a: Requirements, specification, architecture, implementation, integration and test, maintenance.

quiz.q: Define verification and validation in one line each.
quiz.a: Verification: is each artifact built to the specification it was derived from (building the product right)? Validation: does the finished system meet the customer's need (building the right product)?

quiz.q: Why does the V-model plan each test level as soon as its matching design level is written?
quiz.a: Because a test can only be written once the expected behaviour is fixed. Writing the system test alongside the specification exposes untestable or contradictory requirements early, when changing them is cheap.

quiz.q: Give one project type where waterfall fits and one where agile fits, with a reason each.
quiz.a: Waterfall: a safety-critical infusion pump, where requirements are fixed and every change needs full re-verification. Agile: a consumer IoT gadget, where features change between short iterations and time-to-market dominates.

quiz.q: Coding takes 8 weeks and integration takes 4 weeks with no overlap. The team then overlaps them by 2 weeks. Give the combined duration before and after the overlap.
quiz.a: Before: 8 + 4 = 12 weeks. Overlap subtracts 2 weeks once: 12 - 2 = 10 weeks.

quiz.q: A team jumps from requirements straight to coding, skipping architecture. Which defects surface late and why are they expensive?
quiz.a: Interface mismatches between modules, wrong processor or memory choice, and missing real-time budget appear only at integration, when modules meet. By then code is written and tested in isolation, so rework touches many modules at once, and the schedule stage reserved for integration is spent on redesign.

quiz.q: A customer asks for one extra feature four months after release. Trace its path through the life cycle and say why configuration management matters here.
quiz.a: It enters at requirements, passes through specification and architecture impact analysis, implementation, integration and test, then a new release. Configuration management is what lets the team recover the exact source and binary of the shipped version, branch from it, and prove which test results belong to which build.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the EDLC is enforced by tooling: requirement databases that link to test cases, continuous integration servers that build and run unit tests on every commit, and defect trackers that tie faults back to a stage. Safety standards such as IEC 61508 and ISO 26262 formalise the V-model into required work products and reviews, so firmware engineers often meet the life cycle first as a compliance checklist. Automotive teams now add a continuous-deployment loop after release, pushing over-the-air updates through the same test gates. Search next for requirements traceability, stage-gate reviews, and functional safety work products.
